newsitem.title: USA: CSX plan seen benefitting rail industry.
newsitem.headline: CSX plan seen benefitting rail industry.

text.p: CSX Corp's plans to expand and improve its Ohio-Chicago route should boost freight capacity on rail lines between the East and West coasts, analysts said Monday.
They said the move should benefit rail companies on either side of the Midwest because Chicago is the gateway connecting eastern rail lines with those in the West.
"It's one of the biggest cities for rail transportation," said Doug Rockel, rail analyst at Furman Selz. "Every major railroad interconnects with one another through Chicago."
CSX chief executive John Snow announced the plan Monday morning, calling it "one of the most ambitious U.S. rail freight development ventures in modern times."
The company is planning to build more than 100 route miles of new tract and rebuild, upgrade or resurface another 250 miles.
The announcement is a sign that railroads are ready to grow again after more than a decade of decline.

"The number of rail miles have fallen more than 50 percent over the last 16 years. I think we've kind of hit the bottom in terms of shrinking the industry, and we're now talking expanding," Rockel said. "There's a renaissance taking place."
CSX spokesman Tom Hoppin said the Ohio-Chicago line carries about 20 to 25 trains a day and handles more than 40 million gross ton miles of freight a year.
The line should carry about 50 trains daily once the project completed in early 1998, Hoppin said.
In 1996 CSX handled 347 billion gross ton miles of freight system-wide, according to company figures.
Steven Lewins, a rail analyst at Gruntal & Co, said CSX's lines are now 15 percent more circuitous than those of competitor Norfolk Southern.

Analysts said the expansion, which also entails building double and triple track rails, should help CSX become more efficient in moving freight. This should improve its service on time-sensitive shipments handled by trucking firms.
"It fits in with their plan to expand their intermodal business very nicely," Rockel said.
The $220 million project represents a fraction of the $1.2 billion capital budget that CSX has for the 1997-1998 year.
Lewins said the expansion is just one step of the company's efforts to digest Conrail, which it acquired with Norfolk Southern earlier this year.
"In the greater scheme of things, it's just one piece in a very big puzzle that's going get put together in the next five years," Lewins said.
CSX shares closed Monday up 7/8 at 51-1/4. Those of Norfolk Southern closed up 2 at 94-1/4.
